A Discrete Ontology for the Standard Model and Gravity
This manuscript presents Foundational Ternary Dynamics (FTD): a computational framework that motivates the Standard Model gauge groups and computes coupling constants and particle masses from five postulates about a discrete cubic lattice plus three explicit calibration declarations (\(a_\mathrm{phys} \equiv \ell_P\), \(t_\mathrm{phys}\), \(K_B = m_e\)).
The framework postulates a three-dimensional cubic lattice (undefined-boundary, not \(\mathbb{Z}^3\) as completed totality) where each site carries a flux vector \(\mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^3\) and a discrete state \(s \in \{-1, 0, +1\}\) that records when local flux density crosses the manifestation threshold \(K_B\). From the lattice geometry alone — specifically, the decomposition of the 26-neighbor Moore neighborhood into three sublattices (SC, FCC, BCC) — the gauge-group structure \(U(1) \times SU(2) \times SU(3)\) is motivated as a [SELECTION], the master-quadratic root \(x_+ \approx 137.036\) matching \(1/\alpha\) to 1.26 ppm at tree level is a [STRONGLY MOTIVATED CONJECTURE] (the polynomial identity is a [THEOREM]; the physical identification has substantial structural-uniqueness evidence but no derivation chain), and the dimensionless mass ratios are computed; absolute masses are calibration-conditional.

What this manuscript does

Motivates the Standard Model gauge groups from lattice geometry [SELECTION] (Book I)
Computes \(\sim 46\) Standard Model observables; roughly two dozen are [DERIVED] or [THEOREM], the remainder are [PARAMETRIC] (FTD-derived constants substituted into standard QFT formulas) (Book II)
Reconstructs linear spin-2 propagation on the lattice and presents a Deser-iterative bootstrap to nonlinear Einstein equations (currently [SELECTION] / [PARTIAL DERIVED]; see Ch. 15) (Book II)
Frames the measurement problem via algebraic type transition (Type III\(_1\) to Type I) — a structural framing, not a derivation of qualia or a unique mechanism (Book III)
Catalogs dark-matter, vacuum-energy, and proton-decay claims with their current tags (most [SELECTION] or [CONJECTURE]; predictions stated with falsification criteria) (Book III)



What this manuscript does not do

Claim a theory of everything. FTD is a framework with explicit scope limitations.
Derive quark masses from first principles (scheme-dependent; see Ch. 13).
Prove confinement rigorously (see Ch. 18 for the current status).
Bypass the lattice’s violation of continuous diffeomorphism invariance (see Ch. 15).

title: Preface
text:
This work began as a computational experiment: simulate a discrete lattice with ternary states and see what emerges. What emerged was unexpected.
The 26-neighbor Moore neighborhood on the cubic lattice decomposes into three sublattices — simple cubic (6 face-adjacent), face-centered cubic (12 edge-adjacent), and body-centered cubic (8 corner-adjacent). Each sublattice excites a different number of flux components, with the resulting structure motivating the Standard Model gauge group \(U(1) \times SU(2) \times SU(3)\) (the structural derivation is a [SELECTION] argument, not a uniqueness theorem). The BCC sublattice’s eigenvalue — a product of cosines, \(1 - \cos k_1 \cos k_2 \cos k_3\) — connects through Watson’s 1939 integral identity to the lemniscatic constant \(G^* = \Gamma(1/4)/\Gamma(3/4)\) (this is a [THEOREM]: \(W_3 = G^{*\,2}/(2\pi)\)). A self-consistency polynomial with coefficient 16 (the square of the CM-curve automorphism count) has two roots, \(x_+ \approx 137.036\) and \(x_- \approx 3.024\). The polynomial identity itself is a [THEOREM]; the physical identification \(x_+ = 1/\alpha\) and \(x_- \approx N_c\) is a [STRONGLY MOTIVATED CONJECTURE] (1.26 ppm and 0.80% empirical match; supported by Bayes-factor and structural-uniqueness scans).
The framework has five postulates and a derivation chain that produces six dimensionless constants from \(G^*\) alone (the dimensionless predictions: \(\alpha\), \(N_c\), lepton mass ratios, mixing ratios). Three calibration declarations (\(a_\mathrm{phys} \equiv \ell_P\), \(t_\mathrm{phys} = \sqrt{3}\,\ell_P/c\), \(K_B = m_e\)) are required to translate dimensionless ratios into dimensional units; predictions in absolute units are conditional on this calibration. Of the \(\sim 46\) Standard Model observables tracked in Book II, roughly two dozen are [DERIVED] or [THEOREM] (mostly structural integers and ratios) and the remainder are [PARAMETRIC] (FTD-derived constants substituted into standard QFT formulas). The full nonlinear Einstein-equation recovery and the measurement-problem framing via algebraic type transition (Type III\(_1\) to Type I) are presented at their currently-supported tags — a structural framing rather than a complete derivation.
This manuscript is written for working physicists. It assumes familiarity with quantum field theory, general relativity, and lattice gauge theory. Motivation and philosophy are minimal; derivations are explicit. Every claim carries an epistemic tag indicating whether it is a theorem, a selection principle, a conjecture, or an open question.
The author makes no claim that this is the final theory of physics. It is a framework that produces the right numbers from discrete geometry. Whether it is the right framework — or merely a remarkably efficient parametrization — is for the reader to judge. The falsification criteria are in Chapter 24.






NoteMethodology



This work was developed through computationally-guided mathematical discovery (CGMD): systematic lattice simulation revealing structural identities that were then proven analytically. The master quadratic was discovered by simulation, not deduction. The proofs came after.

title: 2  Mathematical Prerequisites
text:
2.1 P.2.1 Discrete differential geometry on \(\mathbb{Z}^3\)
This chapter collects the mathematical tools used throughout the manuscript. The reader is assumed to know quantum field theory, general relativity, and lattice gauge theory. This chapter provides only FTD-specific notation and identities.
The lattice operators on a scalar field \(\phi : \mathbb{Z}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) and vector field \(\mathbf{A} : \mathbb{Z}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3\):
Gradient (forward difference): \[
(\nabla \phi)_\mu(v) = \phi(v + \hat{e}_\mu) - \phi(v)
\tag{P.1}
\]
Divergence: \[
(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{A})(v) = \sum_{\mu=1}^3 \left[ A_\mu(v) - A_\mu(v - \hat{e}_\mu) \right]
\tag{P.2}
\]
Curl: \[
(\nabla \times \mathbf{A})_\mu(v) = \epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho} \left[ A_\rho(v + \hat{e}_\nu) - A_\rho(v) - A_\nu(v + \hat{e}_\rho) + A_\nu(v) \right]
\tag{P.3}
\]
Laplacian (6-neighbor SC stencil): \[
(\nabla^2 \phi)(v) = \sum_{\mu=1}^3 \left[ \phi(v + \hat{e}_\mu) + \phi(v - \hat{e}_\mu) - 2\phi(v) \right]
\tag{P.4}
\]
Laplacian (26-neighbor Moore stencil): \[
(\nabla^2_M \phi)(v) = \sum_{\delta \in N^M(v) \setminus \{v\}} w_\delta \left[ \phi(v + \delta) - \phi(v) \right]
\tag{P.5}
\]
with weights \(w_\delta = 1/|\delta|^2\) (inverse distance squared): \(w_{\text{SC}} = 1\), \(w_{\text{FCC}} = 1/2\), \(w_{\text{BCC}} = 1/3\).

title: 2  Mathematical Prerequisites
text:
2.2 P.2.2 Momentum space
On a periodic \(L \times L \times L\) torus, the crystal momentum takes values \(\mathbf{k} = 2\pi \mathbf{n}/L\) with \(\mathbf{n} \in \{0, 1, \ldots, L-1\}^3\). The lattice Fourier transform:
\[
\tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{k}) = \frac{1}{L^3} \sum_{v} \phi(v) \, e^{-i\mathbf{k} \cdot v}
\tag{P.6}
\]
The lattice momentum squared: \[
\hat{k}^2 = 4 \sum_{\mu=1}^3 \sin^2(k_\mu/2) = 2\sum_\mu (1 - \cos k_\mu)
\tag{P.7}
\]
This is the eigenvalue of \(-\nabla^2\) on the SC stencil.

section: 2.4 P.2.4 Elliptic curves and complex multiplication
text:
2.4 P.2.4 Elliptic curves and complex multiplication
An elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{Q}\) is a smooth projective curve of genus 1 with a rational point. In Weierstrass form: \(E: y^2 = x^3 + ax + b\) with discriminant \(\Delta = -16(4a^3 + 27b^2) \neq 0\).
The \(j\)-invariant: \(j(E) = -1728 \cdot (4a)^3 / \Delta\).
An elliptic curve has complex multiplication (CM) by an imaginary quadratic order \(\mathcal{O}\) if \(\text{End}(E) \cong \mathcal{O}\), rather than \(\text{End}(E) \cong \mathbb{Z}\) (the generic case).
The CM curve relevant to FTD: \[
E_i: y^2 = x^3 - x, \quad j = 1728, \quad \text{End}(E_i) \cong \mathbb{Z}[i]
\tag{P.10}
\]
Automorphism group: \(\text{Aut}(E_i) = \{1, -1, i, -i\} \cong \mathbb{Z}_4\). Order 4. Square: 16.

title: 3  The Five Postulates
text:
3.1 1.1 The postulates
The framework rests on five postulates. Each is minimal: it states what exists and what is permitted, nothing more. The physical content — gauge groups, coupling constants, masses — is not postulated but derived in subsequent chapters.
These five postulates define the arena. The dynamics (the specific update rule) are not postulated but derived from an action principle in Chapter 16.
Proof. Binary \(\{0, 1\}\): fails (1), since pair creation would require \(0 \to 1 + (-1)\) but \(-1 \notin \{0,1\}\). Binary \(\{-1, +1\}\): fails (2), since there is no neutral element. Ternary \(\{-1, 0, +1\}\): satisfies (1) via \(0 \to (+1) + (-1)\), (2) via \(s = 0\) as fixed point, (3) via \((+1) + (-1) = 0\). Quaternary or higher: \(\{-1, 0, +1\}\) already satisfies all three, so no additional states are needed. \(\square\)

text:
3.4 Postulate 3: Ternary states (J-primary; \(s\) as manifestation projection)
Each voxel carries a flux field \(\mathbf{J}(v, t) \in \mathbb{R}^3\) (the dispositional layer) and a discrete state \(s(v, t) \in \{-1, 0, +1\}\) (the manifestation layer). \(\mathbf{J}\) is primary; \(s\) is the action of \(\mathbf{J}\) via the Genesis threshold rule (Postulate 6 / Genesis dynamics): when \(\|\mathbf{J}(v, t)\|\) crosses the manifestation threshold \(K_B\), the void voxel manifests as \(s = \pm 1\) according to the sign of the flux divergence; otherwise \(s = 0\). Thus \(s\) is not an independent field — it is the discrete observable layer that records when \(\mathbf{J}\)’s local intensity crosses \(K_B\). The state \(s = 0\) is the void (substrate awaiting activation); \(s = \pm 1\) are manifestations of opposite charge.
Why this is one postulate, not two: the flux field \(\mathbf{J}\) is the dispositional content of the void substrate (Postulate 1); the ternary state \(s\) is the manifestation projection of \(\mathbf{J}\) via the Genesis rule. Treating \(s\) as primary and \(\mathbf{J}\) as separate would double-count: \(\mathbf{J}\)’s existence is implicit in the void’s dispositional character, and \(s\) is definitionally the threshold-projection of \(\mathbf{J}\), not an independent observable. (See SPEC_FTD.md §1.1 graded-monism table; the ontology was clarified 2026-05-02 in the MC-T4.1 reframe.)

title: 3  The Five Postulates
text:
3.5 Postulate 4: Local causality
The state of a voxel at tick \(t+1\) depends only on the states and fluxes within its Moore neighborhood at tick \(t\): \[
N^M(v) = \{ u \in \mathbb{Z}^3 : \|u - v\|_\infty \leq 1 \}
\] This is the set of 26 neighbors plus the center voxel itself, giving \(|N^M(v)| = 27 = 3^3\). Information propagates at most one lattice unit per tick.

title: 3  The Five Postulates
text:
3.6 Postulate 5: Determinism
Given the complete configuration \((s, \mathbf{J})\) at tick \(t\), the configuration at tick \(t+1\) is uniquely determined. There are no hidden degrees of freedom and no probabilistic elements in the update rule.

title: 3  The Five Postulates
text:
3.7 1.2 Immediate consequences
Several structural facts follow from the postulates alone, before any dynamics are specified.
Finite causal volume. [THEOREM] By Postulate 4, the causal past of any event \((v, t)\) is contained in \(N^M_t(v) = \{ u : \|u - v\|_\infty \leq t \}\), a cube of side \(2t + 1\). The causal volume grows as \((2t+1)^3\), polynomially in \(t\). No infinite regress is possible in finite time.
CFL speed. [THEOREM] The maximum propagation speed is \(c = 1\) voxel/tick in the Chebyshev metric (\(\ell^\infty\) norm). In physical units where the face-adjacent lattice spacing is the unit of length, the CFL speed is \(c = 1/\sqrt{3}\). This arises because the body-diagonal distance is \(\sqrt{3}\) lattice units but is traversed in 1 tick.
Configuration space. [THEOREM] At each tick, the global configuration is a pair \((s, \mathbf{J})\) where \(s : \mathbb{Z}^3 \to \{-1, 0, +1\}\) is the state field and \(\mathbf{J} : \mathbb{Z}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3\) is the flux field (introduced in Chapter 4). On a finite lattice of \(N\) sites, the state field has \(3^N\) configurations. The full configuration space \(\mathcal{A} = \{-1, 0, +1\}^N \times (\mathbb{R}^3)^N\) is hybrid discrete-continuous.

title: 3  The Five Postulates

3.9 Theorem 1.1 (Ternary necessity)
The state space \(\{-1, 0, +1\}\) is the unique minimal set satisfying:

Charge conservation. Pair creation from the void requires \(0 \to (+1) + (-1)\), which needs at least three values: positive, negative, and neutral. Binary \(\{0, 1\}\) cannot represent charge-neutral pair creation.
Stable vacuum. The void state \(s = 0\) must be a fixed point when \(\mathbf{J} = 0\). Binary \(\{-1, +1\}\) has no neutral element; the vacuum is dynamically unstable.
Destructive interference. Annihilation \((+1) + (-1) \to 0\) requires an additive identity that is also a state. This is the ternary axiom \(0 = (-1) + (+1)\).

No state space with fewer than three elements satisfies all three. No state space with more than three is needed, since \(\{-1, 0, +1\}\) is closed under the ternary constraint.

title: 4  The Two-Layer Ontology
text:
4.1 2.1 The state field
The lattice carries two fields: a discrete state field and a continuous flux field. Their interaction — mediated by the Gauss constraint — is the engine of all dynamics.
The state field \(s : \mathbb{Z}^3 \times \mathbb{N} \to \{-1, 0, +1\}\) assigns a ternary value to each voxel at each tick. It is the actual layer: what has manifested. In the language of dispositionalism, the state field records what is the case.
The charge density is the state field itself: \(\rho(v) = s(v)\).
Proof. The divergence operator \(\nabla \cdot : \mathbb{R}^{3N} \to \mathbb{R}^N\) has rank \(N - 1\) on a periodic lattice (the constant vector is in the kernel). The constraint \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} = s\) fixes \(N - 1\) components of \(\mathbf{J}\), leaving \(3N - (N-1) = 2N + 1\) free. \(\square\)

title: 4  The Two-Layer Ontology
text:
4.3 2.3 The Gauss constraint
The two fields are coupled by the Gauss constraint:
\[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}(v) = \rho(v) = s(v)
\tag{2.1}
\]

title: 8  The BCC Eigenvalue and Watson Identity
text:
8.1 6.1 The multiplicative eigenvalue [THEOREM]
This chapter contains the central algebraic identity of FTD: the BCC lattice Green’s function at the origin equals \(G^{*2}/(2\pi)\), connecting the discrete lattice to the lemniscatic constant through a product of Gamma functions. The identity was first computed by Watson (1939) and independently rediscovered in FTD; its sublattice attribution was confirmed numerically in April 2026.
The BCC sublattice Laplacian has a normalized eigenvalue that is a product of cosines:
\[
\sigma_{\text{BCC}}(\mathbf{k}) = 1 - \cos k_1 \cos k_2 \cos k_3
\tag{6.1}
\]
This is structurally distinct from the SC eigenvalue (a sum of cosines) and the FCC eigenvalue (a sum of pairwise products). The distinction is decisive: products factor across axes; sums do not.
Proof. The first equality is Watson (1939), proved by contour integration or by the Chowla-Selberg formula applied to the CM curve \(E_i: y^2 = x^3 - x\). The second equality is algebraic: \[
\frac{G^{*2}}{2\pi} = \frac{[\Gamma(1/4)^2/(\sqrt{2}\pi)]^2}{2\pi} = \frac{\Gamma(1/4)^4}{2\pi^2 \cdot 2\pi} = \frac{\Gamma(1/4)^4}{4\pi^3} \quad \square
\]

8.2 6.2 The Green’s function at the origin [THEOREM]
The BCC lattice Green’s function at the origin on the infinite lattice \(\mathbb{Z}^3\) is:
\[
G_{\text{BCC}}(0) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^3} \int_0^{2\pi} \!\! \int_0^{2\pi} \!\! \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{dk_1 \, dk_2 \, dk_3}{1 - \cos k_1 \cos k_2 \cos k_3}
\tag{6.2}
\]
where the zero modes (four points in the Brillouin zone where \(\sigma_{\text{BCC}} = 0\)) contribute integrable singularities.
crumbs: Book I: The Lattice and Its Algebra

title: 8  The BCC Eigenvalue and Watson Identity
text:
8.3 6.3 The geometric series factorization [THEOREM]
The key step: expand the integrand as a geometric series:
\[
\frac{1}{1 - x} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x^n \quad \text{for } |x| < 1
\tag{6.3}
\]
with \(x = \cos k_1 \cos k_2 \cos k_3\). Since \(|x| \leq 1\) and equals 1 only on a set of measure zero, the series converges almost everywhere:
\[
G_{\text{BCC}}(0) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(2\pi)^3} \int (\cos k_1 \cos k_2 \cos k_3)^n \, d^3k
\tag{6.4}
\]
Because the integrand is a product, it factors across the three axes:
\[
G_{\text{BCC}}(0) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left[ \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} (\cos k)^n \, dk \right]^3
\tag{6.5}
\]
The 1D integral vanishes for odd \(n\). For even \(n = 2m\):
\[
\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} (\cos k)^{2m} \, dk = \frac{1}{4^m} \binom{2m}{m}
\tag{6.6}
\]
Therefore:
\[
G_{\text{BCC}}(0) = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \left[ \frac{1}{4^m} \binom{2m}{m} \right]^3
\tag{6.7}
\]
This is the cube of central binomial coefficients, a classical object in combinatorics and special function theory.
crumbs: Book I: The Lattice and Its Algebra
8  The BCC Eigenvalue and Watson Identity

title: 8  The BCC Eigenvalue and Watson Identity
text:
8.4 6.4 The Watson identity [THEOREM]
The sum of cubed central binomial coefficients evaluates to:
\[
\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \left[ \frac{1}{4^m} \binom{2m}{m} \right]^3 = \frac{\Gamma(1/4)^4}{4\pi^3}
\tag{6.8}
\]
This is Watson’s integral \(I_1\) (Watson, 1939). The connection to \(\Gamma(1/4)\) arises because the central binomial coefficients \(\binom{2m}{m}/4^m \to 1/\sqrt{\pi m}\) asymptotically, and their cube generates a hypergeometric function \({}_3F_2\) that reduces to products of Gamma values at quarter-integer arguments.

title: 9  The Bridge Constant \(G^*\)
text:
9.1 7.1 Definition [THEOREM]
The lemniscatic bridge constant \(G^*\) is the single number that connects the lattice geometry to the physics. It is not a free parameter: it is a ratio of Gamma function values forced by the BCC Watson integral. This chapter defines \(G^*\), proves its key properties, and establishes the CM curve connection.
The two forms in (7.1) are equivalent via the Gamma reflection formula at \(s = 1/4\): \[
\Gamma(1/4)\,\Gamma(3/4) = \frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi/4)} = \pi\sqrt{2}
\]
so \(\Gamma(3/4) = \pi\sqrt{2}/\Gamma(1/4)\), giving \(\Gamma(1/4)/\Gamma(3/4) = \Gamma(1/4)^2/(\sqrt{2}\pi) = G^*\).

title: 9  The Bridge Constant \(G^*\)
text:
9.3 7.2 Relation to the lemniscate constant [THEOREM]
The classical lemniscate constant is:
\[
\varpi = \frac{\Gamma(1/4)^2}{2\sqrt{2\pi}} = 2.6220575\ldots
\tag{7.2}
\]
This is the half-period of the lemniscate of Bernoulli \(r^2 = \cos(2\theta)\), analogous to \(\pi\) being the half-period of the circle \(r = 1\). The relationship:
\[
G^* = \frac{2\varpi}{\sqrt{\pi}} = \frac{\varpi}{\Gamma(1/2)/2}
\tag{7.3}
\]
\(G^*\) is the ratio of the lemniscate period to the circle period (up to normalization). It bridges between the quartic geometry of the lemniscate (\(r^2 = \cos 2\theta\), related to the elliptic curve \(E_i\)) and the quadratic geometry of the circle (\(r = 1\), related to \(\pi\)).

title: 9  The Bridge Constant \(G^*\)
text:
9.4 7.3 The CM curve [THEOREM]
The elliptic curve \(E_i: y^2 = x^3 - x\) has complex multiplication (CM) by the Gaussian integers \(\mathbb{Z}[i]\). This means the endomorphism ring of \(E_i\) is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}[i]\), not just \(\mathbb{Z}\).
Key properties of \(E_i\):

16.1 14.1 The FTD action [THEOREM]
The update rule that governs the lattice dynamics is not postulated. It is derived from an action principle \(\delta S = 0\), whose Euler-Lagrange equations yield the tick cycle. This chapter presents the action, derives the forces, and establishes the Noether symmetries.
The Euclidean action on the lattice is:
\[
S[s, \mathbf{J}] = \sum_v \left[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{flux}}(v) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{manifest}}(v) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{coupling}}(v) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{constraint}}(v) \right]
\tag{14.1}
\]
with four terms:
Flux kinetic term: \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{flux}} = \frac{1}{2} |\nabla \mathbf{J}|^2 = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\mu} |\mathbf{J}(v + \hat{e}_\mu) - \mathbf{J}(v)|^2
\tag{14.2}
\]
Manifestation (Born-Infeld) term: \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{manifest}} = -K_B \sqrt{1 - |\dot{\mathbf{x}}|^2/c^2 - L^2}
\tag{14.3}
\]
where \(\dot{\mathbf{x}}\) is the lattice velocity and \(L\) is the topological latency (gravitational field). This is the Born-Infeld form that enforces the CFL speed limit \(c = 1/\sqrt{3}\).
State-flux coupling: \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{coupling}} = g_c \, s(v) \, \nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}(v)
\tag{14.4}
\]
where \(g_c = \sqrt{\alpha}\) is the coupling constant.
Gauss constraint (Lagrange multiplier): \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{constraint}} = \lambda_G \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}(v) - s(v) \right)^2
\tag{14.5}
\]
enforcing \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} = s\) with multiplier strength \(\lambda_G \gg 1\).

title: 18  Quantum Mechanics from Flux
text:
18.1 16.1 Complexification [THEOREM]
Quantum mechanics is not postulated in FTD. It emerges from the lattice dynamics through three steps: complexification of the flux field via the Gauss constraint, construction of a Hilbert space, and derivation of the Schrodinger equation as the continuum limit of the lattice wave equation.
The Gauss constraint \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} = s\) on the 3-component flux field \(\mathbf{J} = (J_x, J_y, J_z)\) removes one degree of freedom per site (the longitudinal component). In Coulomb gauge (\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}_\perp = 0\)), the remaining two transverse components define a complex amplitude:
\[
\psi(v) = J_x(v) + i \, J_y(v)
\tag{16.1}
\]
This identification is not arbitrary: the Gauss constraint forces the physical degrees of freedom to be transverse, and two real transverse components naturally combine into one complex field. The choice of which two components to combine is a gauge choice (the third is fixed by \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} = s\)).

title: 18  Quantum Mechanics from Flux
text:
18.2 Theorem 16.1 (Complexification)
The Gauss constraint on \(\mathbb{Z}^3\) reduces the physical flux field from \(\mathbb{R}^3\) per site to \(\mathbb{R}^2 \cong \mathbb{C}\) per site. The resulting complex field \(\psi = J_x + iJ_y\) carries a natural \(U(1)\) phase symmetry inherited from rotation in the \((J_x, J_y)\) plane.

section: 18.5 16.4 The Born rule [THEOREM within the framework]
text:
18.5 16.4 The Born rule [THEOREM within the framework]
Four independent derivations of \(P \propto |\psi|^2\):
Derivation 1: Parseval (energy conservation). [THEOREM] The total flux energy on the lattice is \(E = \sum_v |\mathbf{J}(v)|^2\). By Parseval’s theorem, this equals the sum of squared Fourier amplitudes. The energy fraction at site \(v\) is \(|\mathbf{J}(v)|^2 / E = |\psi(v)|^2 / \sum |\psi|^2\). If manifestation probability is proportional to local energy density, then \(P(v) \propto |\psi(v)|^2\).
Derivation 2: Gleason’s theorem. [THEOREM given the Hilbert space] On a Hilbert space of dimension \(\geq 3\), the only probability measure consistent with the lattice structure of projections is \(P(\psi) = \text{Tr}(\rho |\psi\rangle\langle\psi|) = |\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2\). This is Gleason’s theorem (1957), which applies once the Hilbert space (16.2) is established.
Derivation 3: Decision-theoretic. [SELECTION] A rational agent who knows the lattice dynamics and has partial information about the initial conditions should assign credences proportional to \(|\psi|^2\). This follows the Deutsch-Wallace program applied to the deterministic lattice.
Derivation 4: The existence filter. [THEOREM for the algebraic structure] The projection \(E(z) = \text{Re}(z) = (z + \bar{z})/2\) is idempotent (\(E^2 = E\)) and self-adjoint (\(E^\dagger = E\)). For \(|z| = 1\): \(|E(z)|^2 + |E(iz)|^2 = |\text{Re}(z)|^2 + |\text{Im}(z)|^2 = |z|^2\). This reconstructs the Born rule from two orthogonal applications of the existence filter.

title: 18  Quantum Mechanics from Flux
text:
18.6 16.5 Superposition and interference [THEOREM]
The lattice wave equation is linear in \(\mathbf{J}\) (the nonlinearity enters only through the ternary state field \(s\) and the manifestation threshold). For sub-threshold flux (\(|\mathbf{J}| < K_B\), no manifestation), the dynamics are purely linear:
\[
\mathbf{J}_{\text{total}} = \mathbf{J}_1 + \mathbf{J}_2
\tag{16.5}
\]
This is superposition. Interference follows from the complex structure:
\[
|\psi_1 + \psi_2|^2 = |\psi_1|^2 + |\psi_2|^2 + 2\text{Re}(\overline{\psi_1}\psi_2)
\tag{16.6}
\]
The cross-term \(2\text{Re}(\overline{\psi_1}\psi_2)\) is constructive when the relative phase is small and destructive when the relative phase is near \(\pi\). This is the lattice origin of the double-slit pattern.

title: 18  Quantum Mechanics from Flux
text:
18.7 16.6 What QM is, in FTD
Quantum mechanics is the mathematical framework for computing probability distributions over definite outcomes observed by agents with partial access to a deterministic lattice. It is not a fundamental theory but an effective statistical description of the lattice dynamics, analogous to thermodynamics being an effective description of molecular dynamics.
The lattice is always in a definite state \((s, \mathbf{J})\). Bell’s theorem (1964): Any theory satisfying locality + measurement independence gives CHSH parameter \(S \leq 2\). [THEOREM — standard result]
Tsirelson’s bound (1980): Quantum mechanics gives \(S \leq 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.83\) for maximally entangled states at optimal angles. [THEOREM — standard result]

FTD: A deterministic lattice with local causality (Postulate 4). Bell’s theorem applies. \(S \leq 2\) at the substrate level. Confirmed in simulation.
The resolution: \(S \leq 2\) and \(S = 2\sqrt{2}\) describe different description levels of the same system.

19.3 17.3 The three-level mechanism [SELECTION]
The transition from \(S = 2\) (substrate) to \(S = 2\sqrt{2}\) (emergent) proceeds through three stages:

19.3.1 Level 1: Substrate (local, deterministic) [THEOREM]
On the lattice, a pair of particles created from a void event \(0 \to (+1) + (-1)\) carries opposite charges and anti-correlated flux vectors. A measurement along axis \(\hat{a}\) yields \(\pm 1\) via sign projection: \(A = \text{sign}(\mathbf{J}_A \cdot \hat{a})\).
The correlation function for random 3D flux vectors is: \[
E(\hat{a}, \hat{b}) = \langle A \cdot B \rangle = -\frac{2}{\pi}\theta_{ab} + 1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\theta_{ab} = -1 + \frac{2\theta_{ab}}{\pi}
\tag{17.1}
\]
the triangle function. CHSH: \(S \leq 2\). [THEOREM — verified in Monte Carlo]


19.3.2 Level 2: Complexification (Gauss constraint) [SELECTION]
The Gauss constraint reduces the 3D flux \(\mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^3\) to a 2D complex amplitude \(\psi = J_x + iJ_y\) (Chapter 18). The correlation function changes from triangle to cosine:
\[
E(\hat{a}, \hat{b}) = -\cos\theta_{ab}
\tag{17.2}
\]
because the 2D projection induces a \(\pi/2\) phase shift between the two components. The per-particle correlation enhancement is \(\sqrt{2}\) (from the curvature of cosine vs. triangle).


19.3.3 Level 3: Entanglement (sLoop coupling) [SELECTION]
The void event \(0 \to (+1) + (-1)\) creates a pair with shared flux history. The Gauss constraint forces the pair’s transverse flux fields to be anti-correlated: \(\psi_B = -\overline{\psi_A}\) in the complexified description. This is the singlet state:
\[
|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(|+\rangle|-\rangle - |-\rangle|+\rangle\right)
\tag{17.3}
\]
The joint probability distribution is non-factorizable: \(P(A, B | \hat{a}, \hat{b}) \neq P(A | \hat{a}) P(B | \hat{b})\). This non-factorizability, combined with the cosine correlation, produces \(S = 2\sqrt{2}\).

The observer in FTD is not an external entity appended to the physics. It is a structural property of the lattice: any coherent configuration that processes information from its Moore neighborhood and produces structured output is an observer. This chapter formalizes the observer as a \(3^3\) lattice cluster and derives the three observation modes.
Every entity in FTD — whether observer or object — has the same 27-voxel internal architecture. The distinction between observer and object is relational, not structural: an observer is a cluster whose context includes another cluster’s output.
Individuality comes from configuration, not geometry. A void cluster (\(s = 0\) everywhere, \(|\mathbf{J}| \ll K_B\)) has the geometry but no operative capacity. A particle (coherent flux pattern exceeding \(K_B\)) is a cluster with rich internal dynamics. The observer is not any voxel but a coherent structure — a dynamically stabilized pattern.
The coupling is asymmetric: the observer’s context includes the object’s output, but the object’s context does not include the observer’s internal states. The object does not “know” it is being observed. [CONJECTURE]
The transfer function \(\Phi\) mapping object output to observer context is not a new operator. It is the existing lattice dynamics: - For distant clusters (\(d > 2\)): \(\Phi\) is the lattice propagator. Information travels at \(c = 1/\sqrt{3}\). - For overlapping clusters (\(1 \leq d \leq 2\)): \(\Phi\) is the identity on shared voxels. - For self-observation (\(d = 0\)): \(\Phi\) is the tick cycle itself.

For \(d \in \{1,2\}\), at least one voxel is within both clusters’ \(r = 1\) neighborhoods. For \(d > 2\), no overlap exists. \(\square\)

title: 25  The Vacuum Energy Resolution
text:
25.1 23.1 The problem
The cosmological constant problem — a discrepancy of \(10^{123}\) between quantum field theory predictions and observation — is resolved in FTD by the alpha power ladder. The vacuum energy is the 16th power of \(\alpha\) times factors determined by the lattice geometry.
Quantum field theory estimates the vacuum energy density as: \[
\rho_{\text{QFT}} \sim m_P^4 \sim 10^{76} \text{ GeV}^4
\]
Observation (cosmological constant): \[
\rho_\Lambda^{\text{obs}} \sim 10^{-47} \text{ GeV}^4
\]
The ratio is \(\sim 10^{123}\), the most extreme fine-tuning problem in physics.
The exponent 16 is the same \(K = 16\) that appears in the master quadratic — the physical DOF count on the minimal lattice cell. Each degree of freedom contributes one power of \(\alpha\) to the suppression.
Numerically: \[
\rho_\Lambda = (0.511 \text{ MeV})^4 \times (1/137.036)^{16} \times (2.959)^2 \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-47} \text{ GeV}^4
\]
Comparison: \(\rho_\Lambda^{\text{obs}} = 2.17 \times 10^{-47}\) GeV\(^4\). Agreement: \(\sim 1\%\).

title: 25  The Vacuum Energy Resolution
text:
25.4 23.3 Why \(\alpha^{16}\)? [SELECTION]
The vacuum energy arises from the zero-point fluctuations of the flux field \(\mathbf{J}\). On the lattice, these fluctuations are suppressed by the coupling constant at each of the \(K = 16\) physical degrees of freedom:
\[
\rho_\Lambda \propto \left(\frac{g_c^2}{K}\right)^K = \left(\frac{\alpha}{16}\right)^{16} \sim \alpha^{16}
\]
The key: the suppression is exponential in the DOF count, not polynomial. Each DOF contributes a factor of \(\alpha \approx 1/137\), and 16 such factors produce \(\alpha^{16} \approx 10^{-34}\).
Combined with \(m_e^4 \approx 10^{-14}\) GeV\(^4\) and \(G^{*2} \approx 8.75\): \[
10^{-14} \times 10^{-34} \times 8.75 \approx 10^{-47} \text{ GeV}^4
\]
matching observation.
crumbs: Book III: The Observer and the Cosmos

title: 25  The Vacuum Energy Resolution
text:
25.5 23.4 Why not \(m_P^4\)?
The QFT estimate \(\rho \sim m_P^4\) assumes that all modes up to the Planck scale contribute to the vacuum energy. On the lattice, this is incorrect:

The lattice has a natural UV cutoff at the lattice spacing \(a\), but the relevant energy scale is not \(m_P\) (the lattice cutoff) but \(m_e\) (the manifestation threshold \(K_B\)).
The vacuum fluctuations are sub-threshold (\(|\mathbf{J}| < K_B\)), so they do not manifest. Only the residual vacuum energy — the energy of fluctuations that are too small to crystallize — contributes to \(\rho_\Lambda\).
The number of independent fluctuation modes that contribute is \(K = 16\), not the astronomically large number assumed in QFT.

The \(10^{123}\) discrepancy is not a fine-tuning problem; it is a counting error: QFT counts modes that the lattice structure does not permit.

title: 28  The Periodic Table
text:
28.1 A Personal Inventory
“All the elements, from hydrogen to uranium and beyond”
Consider what you are made of. The calcium in your bones was forged in the heart of a dying star. The iron in your blood, every atom, was created in the final moments before a supernova. The oxygen you breathe was released by cyanobacteria that lived two billion years before you were born.
You are not merely in the universe. You are the universe, organized into a pattern that can contemplate itself.
The periodic table is the census of that organization: 118 ways that protons, neutrons, and electrons arrange themselves into stable patterns. Each element is not just a chemical species: it is a chapter in the story of cosmic evolution, from the first three minutes after the Big Bang to the stellar explosions that seeded your planet with complexity.

title: 28  The Periodic Table
text:
NoteHistorical Context





Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869, famously predicting undiscovered elements (gallium, scandium, germanium) from gaps in his arrangement. The physical basis: electron shells: came only after quantum mechanics (Bohr 1913, Schrödinger 1926). Glenn Seaborg expanded the table with actinides in the 1940s. Today’s 118 elements represent configurations from 1 proton (hydrogen) to 118 (oganesson), with each row reflecting a new electron shell being filled.

title: 28  The Periodic Table
text:
28.2 The Logic of the Table
The periodic table organizes elements by: - Rows (periods): Shell being filled - Columns (groups): Valence electron configuration - Blocks: Orbital type (s, p, d, f)






NoteMass Units in This Chapter



Atomic masses are given in atomic mass units (u), where 1 u = 1/12 the mass of carbon-12 ≈ 931.5 MeV/c². The mass of a hydrogen atom is approximately 1 u, making these values easy to interpret: they roughly equal the nucleon count (protons + neutrons).

28.3.1 Hydrogen: The First Atom
Three minutes after the Big Bang, when the universe had cooled enough for protons and electrons to exist, the first hydrogen atoms formed. Not forged in any star: hydrogen predates stars. Every hydrogen atom in the water you drink is approximately 13.8 billion years old, unchanged since the beginning.






Figure 28.1: Hydrogen: the simplest atom, consisting of one proton and one electron in the 1s orbital.



The hydrogen in your body has been on an extraordinary journey: first floating in primordial gas clouds, then compressed into the first stars, then ejected in stellar winds, then gathered into the solar nebula, then incorporated into water on Earth, then drunk by countless organisms before you. Yet it remains, at its core, the same simple pattern: one proton, one electron: that formed when the universe was three minutes old.


28.3.2 Helium: The Inert Witness






Figure 28.2: Helium: two protons, two neutrons, and two electrons filling the 1s shell completely: making it chemically inert.



Helium has a closed shell and participates in no chemistry. It witnesses the universe but does not engage. The helium in a party balloon was mostly made in the Big Bang or fused in stellar cores. It escapes Earth’s atmosphere (too light to be held by our gravity) and drifts into space. We will eventually run out of helium on Earth; it is not renewable.

28.4.1 Carbon: The Element of Life
There is something miraculous about carbon-12: three helium nuclei fused together in the heart of a red giant star. This fusion is exquisitely improbable: requiring a quantum resonance (the Hoyle state) at exactly the right energy. If that resonance were 4% different, carbon would not form; if it were 1% different, carbon would not survive to be ejected into space. We exist because of a 1% window in nuclear physics.
Carbon has 4 valence electrons, allowing it to form 4 bonds. This versatility enables: - Long chains (hydrocarbons) - Rings (aromatic compounds) - Complex structures (proteins, DNA)
The carbon in your DNA was once inside a star. That star died, and its carbon drifted through space for millions of years. It condensed into the cloud that became our solar system, aggregated into Earth, was cycled through the atmosphere and oceans, was absorbed by plants, eaten by animals, and eventually became you: a pattern of carbon atoms that can read about carbon atoms.

Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon. Stars cannot gain energy by fusing iron: it is the end of the fusion line. When a massive star’s core becomes iron, fusion stops, and the star collapses in milliseconds, triggering a supernova.
In that catastrophic moment: lasting less than a second: elements heavier than iron are forged: gold, platinum, uranium. These heavy elements exist only because stars die violently. The gold in a wedding ring required a star to explode.
The iron in your blood (each hemoglobin molecule carries four iron atoms) was synthesized in the final moments of a star’s life, blasted across space at 10% the speed of light, incorporated into the cloud that became our solar system, and eventually found its way into you. You are, quite literally, a walking supernova remnant.






NoteThe Cosmic Origin of Blood



Every breath you take, the iron in your hemoglobin carries oxygen from your lungs to your cells. That iron was forged in a stellar core over 5 billion years ago. When you cut yourself and see red, you are seeing the signature of a dead star.

title: 29  Electron Dynamics
text:
29.1 Shell Filling Rules
“How electrons orbit, bond, and determine chemistry”

title: 29  Electron Dynamics
text:
29.1.1 Aufbau Principle
Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy, following the Aufbau sequence:

1s \(\to\) 2s \(\to\) 2p \(\to\) 3s \(\to\) 3p \(\to\) 4s \(\to\) 3d \(\to\) 4p \(\to\) 5s \(\to\) 4d \(\to\) 5p \(\to\) 6s \(\to\) 4f \(\to\) 5d \(\to\) 6p \(\to\) 7s \(\to\) 5f \(\to\) 6d \(\to\) 7p

Note that 4s fills before 3d because it has lower energy at this point in the sequence.


29.1.2 Pauli Exclusion
No two electrons can have identical quantum numbers.
In simulation: same-state particles repel at short range, preventing overlap.


29.1.3 Hund’s Rule
Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly before pairing.
Why? Parallel spins minimize electron-electron repulsion.

title: 29  Electron Dynamics
text:
29.2 Orbital Mechanics

29.2.1 Angular Momentum
Orbital angular momentum is quantized: \[
L = \sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)} \hbar
\]
where \(\ell\) is the azimuthal quantum number (0, 1, 2, 3… for s, p, d, f orbitals respectively).






NoteQuantum Numbers




Principal quantum number \(n\) (1, 2, 3…) determines energy level
Azimuthal quantum number \(\ell\) (0 to n-1) determines orbital shape and angular momentum
Magnetic quantum number \(m_\ell\) (-\(\ell\) to +\(\ell\)) determines orbital orientation
Spin quantum number \(m_s\) (\(\pm 1/2\)) determines electron spin



In simulation: stable orbits occur where angular momentum satisfies the quantization condition.


29.2.2 Energy Levels
For hydrogen-like atoms: \[
E_n = -\frac{13.6 \times Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}
\]
Where Z is the atomic number and n is the principal quantum number.


29.2.3 Probability Distributions
Orbitals define where electrons are likely to be:

title: 29  Electron Dynamics
text:
29.3 Ionization and Electron Affinity

29.3.1 Ionization
Removing an electron requires energy: \[
\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+ + e^-
\]
First ionization energy varies across the table: - Alkali metals: Low (easy to remove) - Noble gases: High (hard to remove)


29.3.2 Electron Affinity
Adding an electron releases energy: \[
\text{Cl} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}^-
\]
Halogens have high electron affinity: they want one more electron to complete their shell.

title: 29  Electron Dynamics
text:
29.4 Valence and Reactivity

29.4.1 Valence Electrons
Electrons in the outermost shell. Determine: - Chemical reactivity - Bond formation - Ion charge


29.4.2 The Octet Rule
Atoms are most stable with 8 valence electrons (full \(s^2 p^6\)).
Atoms achieve this by: - Losing electrons (metals): Na \(\to\) Na\(^+\) - Gaining electrons (nonmetals): Cl \(\to\) Cl\(^-\) - Sharing electrons (covalent): C-C bonds

title: 29  Electron Dynamics
text:
29.5 Transitions and Spectra
When electrons change energy levels:

29.5.1 Absorption
\[
E_{\text{photon}} = E_{\text{final}} - E_{\text{initial}}
\] Electron absorbs photon, jumps to higher energy.


29.5.2 Emission
\[
E_{\text{photon}} = E_{\text{initial}} - E_{\text{final}}
\] Electron emits photon, drops to lower energy.


29.5.3 Spectral Lines
Each element has unique energy levels, creating unique spectral fingerprints.

title: 29  Electron Dynamics
text:
29.6 Spin
Electrons have intrinsic angular momentum (spin): - Spin up: \(+1/2\) - Spin down: \(-1/2\)
Two electrons can share an orbital only if they have opposite spin.

title: 30  Nuclear Physics
text:
30.1 Nuclear Binding
“Fusion, fission, and the power of the nucleus”
The nucleus is held together by the strong force, despite the electromagnetic repulsion between protons.

title: 30  Nuclear Physics
text:
30.1.1 Binding Energy
\[
B = (Z \times m_p + N \times m_n - M_{\text{nucleus}}) \times c^2
\]
The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of its parts. The “missing” mass is the binding energy.


30.1.2 Binding Energy per Nucleon
The curve of binding energy reveals nuclear stability:






Figure 30.1: Nuclear binding energy curve showing Fe-56 at the peak of stability.



Iron-56 sits at the peak with the highest binding energy per nucleon. Lighter elements (like hydrogen) can fuse to release energy by climbing up the curve. Heavier elements (like uranium) can fission to release energy by sliding down from the heavy end.

title: 30  Nuclear Physics
section: 30.2 FTD Derivation: The Semi-Empirical Mass Formula
text:
30.2 FTD Derivation: The Semi-Empirical Mass Formula
The binding energy of nuclei follows the semi-empirical mass formula (Bethe-Weizsäcker). In FTD, each term has a clear geometric origin.

30.2.1 The Formula
\[B(A,Z) = a_V A - a_S A^{2/3} - a_C \frac{Z(Z-1)}{A^{1/3}} - a_A \frac{(A-2Z)^2}{A} + \delta\]
Where: - A = mass number (protons + neutrons) - Z = atomic number (protons) - δ = pairing term


30.2.2 FTD Relations for Coefficients






WarningEpistemic Status: Numerical Relations



The formulas below express the semi-empirical mass formula coefficients using framework integers. These achieve <2% accuracy but represent numerical fits using the same integers that appear elsewhere in FTD, not derivations from first principles. The physical interpretations (saturation, boundary effects, etc.) are motivated by standard nuclear physics; the FTD contribution is expressing the coefficients in terms of K_B, α, N_c, and n_eff.

NoteConsistency, Not Derivation



These relations achieve <2% accuracy using the same integers (K_B, α, N_c, n_eff) that appear in particle masses and coupling constants. This suggests underlying consistency, though why these specific combinations should govern nuclear binding remains an open question.




30.2.3 Volume Term: Strong Force Saturation
The strong force is short-range (Yukawa form). Each nucleon interacts only with nearest neighbors. The binding energy is proportional to the number of nucleons:
\[a_V = K_B \times n_{\text{eff}} = 0.511 \times 30.9 \approx 15.8 \text{ MeV}\]
The factor n_eff ≈ 30.9 comes from the number of flux modes within the nuclear volume.


30.2.4 Surface Term: Boundary Effects
Nucleons at the surface have fewer neighbors → less binding. The surface area scales as A^(2/3):
\[a_S = a_V \times f_{\text{surface}} \approx 18.3 \text{ MeV}\]


30.2.5 Coulomb Term: Electromagnetic Repulsion
Protons repel each other. The Coulomb energy of a uniformly charged sphere:
\[a_C = \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{\alpha \hbar c}{r_0} = \frac{3}{5} \times \alpha \times K_B \times \frac{5}{3} \approx 0.71 \text{ MeV}\]


30.2.6 Asymmetry Term: Pauli Blocking
The Pauli exclusion principle (from spinor structure; see Ch. 16 in the restructured manuscript) requires fermions to occupy different states. Asymmetric nuclei (N ≠ Z) waste energy:
\[a_A = \frac{K_B}{N_c} = \frac{0.511 \text{ MeV}}{3} \times 136 \approx 23.2 \text{ MeV}\]

text:

Certain nuclei are extraordinarily stable: Z or N = 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126

30.3.1 FTD Explanation: Flux Standing Waves
In FTD, nuclear stability corresponds to closed flux shells: standing wave patterns that fill completely:

30.3.2 Doubly Magic Nuclei
Nuclei with both Z AND N magic are exceptionally stable: - \(^4\)He (Z=2, N=2) : “alpha particle” - \(^{16}\)O (Z=8, N=8) - \(^{40}\)Ca (Z=20, N=20) - \(^{208}\)Pb (Z=82, N=126)

title: 30  Nuclear Physics
section: 30.4 The Strong Force in the Nucleus
text:
30.4 The Strong Force in the Nucleus

30.4.1 Properties

Range: ~1-2 fm (1-2 voxels at nuclear scale)
Strength: 100× stronger than EM
Behavior: Attractive at medium range, repulsive at very short range
Carrier: Gluons (between quarks), pions (between nucleons)



30.4.2 Yukawa Potential
\[
V(r) = -g^2 \frac{e^{-mr}}{r}
\]
This short-range potential explains why the strong force dominates only at nuclear distances.

title: 30  Nuclear Physics
text:
30.5 Radioactive Decay
Unstable nuclei transform to reach stability.

30.5.1 Alpha Decay (Heavy Nuclei)
\[
^{238}\text{U} \rightarrow ^{234}\text{Th} + ^{4}\text{He}
\]
A helium nucleus (alpha particle) tunnels through the Coulomb barrier.


30.5.2 Beta Minus Decay (Neutron-Rich)
\[
n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e
\]
A neutron converts to a proton, emitting an electron and antineutrino.


30.5.3 Beta Plus Decay (Proton-Rich)
\[
p \rightarrow n + e^+ + \nu_e
\]
A proton converts to a neutron, emitting a positron and neutrino.


30.5.4 Gamma Decay
\[
\text{Nucleus}^* \rightarrow \text{Nucleus} + \gamma
\]
Excited nucleus releases energy as a photon, no transmutation.

title: 30  Nuclear Physics
text:
30.6 Fusion
Combining light nuclei to make heavier ones.

30.6.1 Requirements

High temperature: Overcome Coulomb barrier
High density: Collision probability
Confinement time: Long enough to react



30.6.2 Proton-Proton Chain (Sun)
\[
4p \rightarrow ^{4}\text{He} + 2e^+ + 2\nu_e + \text{energy}
\]
Step by step:
p + p → D + e⁺ + νₑ      (slow, determines rate)
D + p → ³He + γ
³He + ³He → ⁴He + 2p


30.6.3 CNO Cycle (Massive Stars)
Carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen catalyze hydrogen fusion:
¹²C + p → ¹³N + γ
¹³N → ¹³C + e⁺ + νₑ
¹³C + p → ¹⁴N + γ
¹⁴N + p → ¹⁵O + γ
¹⁵O → ¹⁵N + e⁺ + νₑ
¹⁵N + p → ¹²C + ⁴He
Net: 4p → ⁴He (carbon recycled)

title: 30  Nuclear Physics
text:
30.7 Fission
Splitting heavy nuclei into lighter ones.

30.7.1 Induced Fission
\[
^{235}\text{U} + n \rightarrow ^{141}\text{Ba} + ^{92}\text{Kr} + 3n + 200 \text{ MeV}
\]


30.7.2 Chain Reaction
The 3 neutrons produced can trigger 3 more fissions: - Controlled: Nuclear reactor - Uncontrolled: Nuclear bomb


30.7.3 Critical Mass
Minimum amount needed to sustain chain reaction. Depends on: - Geometry (sphere minimizes surface/volume) - Density - Neutron absorption

title: 30  Nuclear Physics
text:
30.8 Nuclear Energy

30.8.1 Fusion Energy
\[
E = \Delta m \times c^2 = 0.7\% \text{ of mass converted}
\]
Sun converts 4 million tons of mass to energy per second.


30.8.2 Fission Energy
\[
E \approx 200 \text{ MeV per fission}
\]
1 kg of U-235 releases energy equivalent to 20,000 tons of TNT.

title: 31  Chemical Bonds
text:
31.1 Why Atoms Bond
With stable atoms in hand, we now explore how they combine through electron shell interactions.
“How atoms connect”
Atoms are most stable with full outer shells. Most atoms do not have full shells naturally, so they bond with other atoms to share electrons.

title: 31  Chemical Bonds
text:
31.2 Ionic Bonds
Electron transfer creates oppositely charged ions that attract.

31.2.1 Example: Sodium Chloride
Na → Na⁺ + e⁻     (loses 1 electron)
Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻     (gains 1 electron)
Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl  (electrostatic attraction)


31.2.2 Properties of Ionic Compounds

High melting points (strong electrostatic bonds)
Brittle crystals (shift and like charges repel)
Conduct electricity when dissolved (free ions)
Form regular lattice structures

title: 31  Chemical Bonds
text:
31.3 Covalent Bonds
Electron sharing between atoms.

31.3.1 Single Bond
One shared electron pair:
H-H: Each H contributes 1 electron
     Both have 2 electrons (full 1s shell)


31.3.2 Double Bond
Two shared pairs:
O=O: Each O contributes 2 electrons
     Both have 8 valence electrons


31.3.3 Triple Bond
Three shared pairs:
N≡N: Each N contributes 3 electrons
     Very strong, very stable (atmosphere)


31.3.4 Bond Strength
Triple > Double > Single
The more electrons shared, the stronger and shorter the bond.

title: 31  Chemical Bonds
text:
31.4 Polar vs Nonpolar Covalent

31.4.1 Nonpolar Covalent
Equal sharing between identical atoms:
H-H, O=O, N≡N


31.4.2 Polar Covalent
Unequal sharing between different atoms:
H-Cl: Chlorine pulls electrons more strongly
      Creates partial charges: Hδ⁺-Clδ⁻


31.4.3 Electronegativity
The tendency to attract electrons. Fluorine is highest (4.0).
Electronegativity difference determines bond type: - 0-0.4: Nonpolar covalent - 0.4-1.7: Polar covalent - >1.7: Ionic

title: 31  Chemical Bonds
text:
31.5 Metallic Bonds
Electron “sea” shared among many nuclei.

31.5.1 Model
⊕ e⁻ ⊕ e⁻ ⊕ e⁻ ⊕
e⁻ ⊕ e⁻ ⊕ e⁻ ⊕ e⁻
⊕ e⁻ ⊕ e⁻ ⊕ e⁻ ⊕

⊕ = metal cation
e⁻ = delocalized electron


31.5.2 Properties of Metals

Electrical conductivity (electrons move freely)
Thermal conductivity (electrons carry heat)
Malleability (layers slide without breaking bonds)
Metallic luster (electrons reflect light)

title: 31  Chemical Bonds
text:
31.6 Hydrogen Bonds
Weak bonds between molecules, crucial for life.

31.6.1 Formation
When H is bonded to N, O, or F (electronegative atoms):
H-O-H ··· H-O-H
         ↑
    Hydrogen bond


31.6.2 Strength
About 5% of a covalent bond. Weak individually, but significant collectively.


31.6.3 Importance

Water’s high boiling point
DNA double helix structure
Protein secondary structure
Ice floating (unusual: lower density solid)

title: 31  Chemical Bonds
text:
31.7 Van der Waals Forces
Weakest intermolecular forces.

31.7.1 London Dispersion
Temporary dipoles from electron fluctuations. Present in ALL molecules.


31.7.2 Dipole-Dipole
Permanent dipoles attract each other.


31.7.3 Dipole-Induced Dipole
Permanent dipole induces temporary dipole in neighbor.

title: 35  States of Matter
text:
35.6 Temperature in Simulation
Temperature emerges from particle motion. In FTD, we define a temperature proxy that mirrors the kinetic theory result:
\[
T_{\text{proxy}} = \frac{\langle|\mathbf{J}|^2\rangle}{3N}
\]






NoteDimensional Analysis



In physical units, kinetic theory gives \(\frac{3}{2}k_B T = \frac{1}{2}m\langle v^2\rangle\), so \(T = \frac{m\langle v^2\rangle}{3k_B}\). In FTD natural units where flux \(|J|\) serves as a momentum proxy and we set \(k_B = 1\), the temperature proxy has dimensions of energy per particle. The factor of 3 accounts for three spatial dimensions (equipartition theorem).


Higher average squared flux magnitude = higher temperature.

title: 35  States of Matter
text:
35.7 Pressure in Simulation
Pressure from particle collisions with boundaries:
\[
P = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{\text{momentum transfer}}{\text{area} \times \text{time}}
\]

35.10 Concepts

liquid: Touching, flowing, short-range order
gas: Separated, free motion
plasma: Ionized gas







NoteChapter Summary



Matter exists in four primary phases: solid (fixed positions, long-range order), liquid (touching but mobile, short-range order), gas (separated, no order), and plasma (ionized, responds to fields). Temperature emerges as average kinetic flux: T_proxy = \(\langle|J|^2\rangle\)/3N. Phase is determined by density, temperature proxy, and correlation length. The same atoms behave completely differently depending on conditions: phase is about motion, not identity. Plasma is the most common state in the universe (99% of visible matter is in stars).

36.3 Latent Heat
Energy absorbed or released during transition without temperature change.

36.3.1 Heat of Fusion
Energy to melt solid: \[
Q = m \times L_f
\]


36.3.2 Heat of Vaporization
Energy to boil liquid: \[

\]

title: 36  Phase Transitions
text:
36.4 First-Order Transitions
Sharp boundaries, latent heat involved.

36.4.1 Characteristics

Discontinuity in first derivative of free energy
Coexisting phases at transition
Latent heat required
Examples: Melting, boiling, sublimation

title: 36  Phase Transitions
text:
36.5 Second-Order Transitions
Continuous change, no latent heat.

36.5.1 Characteristics

Discontinuity in second derivative of free energy
No latent heat
Order parameter changes continuously
Examples: Ferromagnetic → paramagnetic, superconducting transition

title: 36  Phase Transitions
text:
36.6 The Clausius-Clapeyron Equation
Describes the slope of phase boundaries:
\[
\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{L}{T \Delta V}
\]
Where: - L = latent heat - ΔV = volume change

36.6.1 Water’s Anomaly
Ice is less dense than water (ΔV < 0), so melting curve has negative slope. Higher pressure → lower melting point.

title: 36  Phase Transitions
text:
36.7 Nucleation
Transitions do not happen uniformly: they start at nucleation sites.

36.7.1 Homogeneous Nucleation
Random fluctuations create seeds of new phase. Rare.


36.7.2 Heterogeneous Nucleation
Impurities or surfaces provide sites. Much more common.


36.7.3 Supercooling/Superheating
Without nucleation sites, matter can exist past transition temperature: - Supercooled water: Liquid below 0°C - Superheated liquid: Liquid above boiling point

title: 36  Phase Transitions
text:
36.8 Critical Phenomena
Near the critical point: - Fluctuations become huge - Properties diverge (critical opalescence) - No distinction between liquid and gas
Above the critical point: supercritical fluid: properties of both liquid and gas.

title: 36  Phase Transitions
text:
36.9 Cosmological Phase Transitions
The early universe underwent phase transitions just like water, but at vastly higher temperatures.

36.9.1 The Electroweak Transition (T ~ 100 GeV)
At T ~ 10¹⁵ K (100 GeV), the Higgs field condensed:



Before
After




\(\langle H \rangle = 0\)
\(\langle H \rangle = 246\) GeV


W, Z massless
W, Z massive


EM and Weak unified
EM and Weak separate



In FTD: This is a first-order transition. It proceeds via bubble nucleation: exactly like water boiling, but with the Higgs condensate forming inside bubbles.
The bubble walls are where baryogenesis happens (see Chapter 10.4).


36.9.2 The QCD Transition (T ~ 150 MeV)
At T ~ 10¹² K (150 MeV), quarks and gluons confined into hadrons:



Before
After




Quark-gluon plasma
Protons, neutrons, pions


Free quarks
Quarks confined in color-neutral combinations


\(\chi\) symmetry intact
\(\chi\) symmetry spontaneously broken



In FTD: This is a crossover (smooth transition), not first-order. The flux configurations reorganize continuously rather than via bubbles.

All phase transitions in FTD involve the flux field reorganizing:

text:
39.2 Properties Explained

39.2.1 Electrical Conductivity
Electrons move freely in response to electric field: \[
\mathbf{J} = \sigma \mathbf{E}
\]
Current flows because electrons can move without jumping between atoms.


39.2.2 Thermal Conductivity
Electrons carry heat: \[
\kappa = \frac{1}{3} C_v v \lambda
\]
Metals conduct heat well because electrons move fast and far.


39.2.3 Malleability and Ductility
Layers of ions can slide past each other without breaking bonds: the electron sea reforms around the new positions. When force is applied, atomic planes can shift while maintaining metallic bonding, unlike ionic or covalent solids that would shatter.


39.2.4 Metallic Luster
Free electrons oscillate in response to light and re-emit it: metals are shiny.


39.2.5 Opacity
Electrons absorb photons across a continuous range: metals are opaque.

title: 39  Metals and Conductors
text:
39.3 Band Theory
A more sophisticated view of electron behavior.

39.3.1 Energy Bands

Valence band: Filled electron states
Conduction band: Empty or partially filled states
Band gap: Energy difference between bands



39.3.2 Metal Band Structure






Figure 39.2: Metal band structure: overlapping valence and conduction bands with no energy gap, allowing free electron movement.



In metals, the valence and conduction bands overlap or touch, with the conduction band being partially filled. There is no energy gap, so electrons can move freely in response to applied fields.

title: 39  Metals and Conductors
text:
39.4 Resistance
Even metals have some resistance.

39.4.1 Sources

Phonon scattering: Vibrating atoms deflect electrons
Impurity scattering: Foreign atoms deflect electrons
Defect scattering: Lattice imperfections deflect electrons



39.4.2 Temperature Dependence
\[
\rho(T) = \rho_0 (1 + \alpha T)
\]
Resistance increases with temperature (more phonons).

title: 39  Metals and Conductors

39.6 Free Electron Model
Treating electrons as non-interacting particles.

39.6.1 Fermi Energy
Maximum electron energy at absolute zero: \[
E_F = \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\frac{3\pi^2 n}{V}\right)^{2/3}
\]


39.6.2 Fermi Velocity
\[
v_F = \sqrt{\frac{2E_F}{m}} \approx 10^6 \text{ m/s}
\]
Electrons at the Fermi surface move very fast.


39.6.3 Fermi-Dirac Distribution
Probability of state being occupied: \[
f(E) = \frac{1}{e^{(E-E_F)/k_BT} + 1}
\]
At T = 0, sharp cutoff at \(E_F\).

title: 40  Semiconductors
text:
40.2 Intrinsic Semiconductors
Pure silicon or germanium.

40.2.1 Band Structure






Figure 40.1: Semiconductor band structure: a moderate energy gap (1.1 eV for silicon) separates the filled valence band from the empty conduction band.



At absolute zero, the valence band is completely filled and the conduction band is empty. The band gap (1.1 eV for silicon) determines the semiconductor’s properties.


40.2.2 Thermal Excitation
At T > 0, some electrons gain enough energy to jump the gap: \[
n = n_0 \exp\left(-\frac{E_g}{2k_BT}\right)
\]


40.2.3 Carriers

Electrons: Negative carriers in conduction band
Holes: Positive carriers in valence band (missing electrons)

Both contribute to conductivity.

title: 40  Semiconductors
text:
40.3 Doping
Adding impurities to control carrier concentration.

40.3.1 n-Type (Add Group V: P, As, Sb)






Figure 40.2: n-type doping: a Group V atom (like phosphorus) in a silicon lattice provides one extra electron.



Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons. Four bond with silicon neighbors, leaving one extra electron free to conduct.


40.3.2 p-Type (Add Group III: B, Ga, Al)






Figure 40.3: p-type doping: a Group III atom (like boron) in a silicon lattice creates one hole (missing electron).



Boron has only 3 valence electrons. It bonds with four silicon neighbors, leaving one hole that can accept an electron.


40.3.3 Carrier Concentrations
For n-type: \(n >> p\), electrons dominate For p-type: \(p >> n\), holes dominate

title: 40  Semiconductors
text:
40.4 The p-n Junction
Interface between p-type and n-type regions.

40.4.1 Formation






Figure 40.4: The p-n junction: when p-type and n-type semiconductors meet, electrons and holes recombine at the interface, creating a depletion zone.



At the junction, electrons from the n-side diffuse into the p-side and recombine with holes. This creates a depletion zone: a region with no free carriers, only fixed charged ions (negative on p-side, positive on n-side).


40.4.2 Depletion Zone
Region with no free carriers. Acts as insulator.


40.4.3 Built-in Voltage
Electric field from exposed ions creates potential barrier.

title: 40  Semiconductors
text:
40.5 Diode Behavior

40.5.1 Forward Bias (+ on p-side)
Shrinks depletion zone. Current flows.


40.5.2 Reverse Bias (+ on n-side)
Expands depletion zone. No current (blocking).


40.5.3 I-V Characteristic
\[
I = I_0 \left(e^{qV/k_BT} - 1\right)
\]
Exponential in forward direction, blocked in reverse.

title: 40  Semiconductors
text:
40.6 Transistor
The switch that enables computing.

40.6.1 Basic Types

BJT (Bipolar Junction Transistor): npn or pnp
MOSFET (Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor FET): Most common today



40.6.2 MOSFET Structure






Figure 40.5: MOSFET structure: gate voltage controls the conductivity of the channel between source and drain.



The Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor has three terminals: source, drain, and gate. Applying voltage to the gate creates (or removes) a conducting channel between source and drain.


40.6.3 Switching

Gate voltage low: Channel off (insulating)
Gate voltage high: Channel on (conducting)

This is how 0s and 1s are represented.

title: 40  Semiconductors
text:
40.7 In Simulation
class Semiconductor:
    def __init__(self, base_material, dopant_type, dopant_concentration):
        self.material = base_material
        self.type = dopant_type
        self.carrier_density = calculate_carriers(dopant_concentration)

    def conductivity(self, temperature, electric_field):
        # Intrinsic carriers
        n_i = intrinsic_carrier(self.material, temperature)

        # Doped carriers
        if self.type == N_TYPE:
            n = self.carrier_density
            p = n_i**2 / n
        else:
            p = self.carrier_density
            n = n_i**2 / p

        return ELECTRON_MOBILITY * n + HOLE_MOBILITY * p

title: 42  Gravity Wells
text:
42.4 General Relativity: Emergence from FTD
In FTD, gravity is a force arising from density gradients:
\[\mathbf{F}_g = G_{\text{bias}} \cdot \nabla\bar{\rho}(x)\]
But general relativity describes gravity as spacetime curvature. How do these connect?

42.4.1 The Effective Metric
The flux density field ρ(x) creates an effective metric:
\[g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu} + h_{\mu\nu}(\rho)\]
Where: - η_μν is the flat Minkowski metric - h_μν is the perturbation from flux density
In the weak-field limit:
\[h_{00} = -\frac{2\Phi}{c^2}, \quad h_{ij} = -\frac{2\Phi}{c^2}\delta_{ij}\]
Where Φ is the Newtonian potential, related to flux density by:
\[\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G \rho\]


42.4.2 Geodesic Motion
Free particles in FTD follow flux gradients. In the GR picture, this is geodesic motion:
\[\frac{d^2x^\mu}{d\tau^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\nu\lambda}\frac{dx^\nu}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\lambda}{d\tau} = 0\]
The Christoffel symbols Γ are determined by the metric derivatives: which come from the flux density profile.






NoteGravity as Geometry



FTD’s flux gradients create an effective curved geometry. What looks like a force is actually motion along the straightest possible path (geodesic) in curved spacetime.




42.4.3 Einstein’s Equations
The linearized Einstein equations:
\[\Box h_{\mu\nu} = -16\pi G T_{\mu\nu}\]
emerge from the FTD wave equation for the flux field:
\[\partial_t^2 J = c^2 \nabla^2 J + \text{sources}\]
The stress-energy tensor T_μν corresponds to the flux density and momentum distributions.


42.4.4 Beyond Linearized Gravity
At higher flux densities (strong gravity), nonlinear effects appear: - Metric perturbations interact with each other - Geodesic deviation becomes significant - Full Einstein equations emerge
This is why FTD naturally incorporates: - Gravitational waves (flux ripples) - Black holes (extreme flux concentrations) - Cosmological expansion (large-scale flux dynamics)


42.4.5 Gravitational Waves in FTD
When massive objects accelerate, flux patterns propagate outward:
\[h_{+,\times} \propto \frac{1}{r}\frac{d^2Q_{ij}}{dt^2}\]
These are gravitational waves: transverse ripples in the flux field traveling at speed C.

43.3 The Greenhouse Effect






Figure 43.1: Atmospheric structure and the greenhouse mechanism: sunlight penetrates to the surface, which emits infrared radiation that is partially trapped by atmospheric gases.




43.3.1 Mechanism
Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the ground. The warmed surface emits infrared radiation, which greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb and re-emit in all directions, including back toward the surface. This traps heat and raises the surface temperature above what it would be without an atmosphere.


43.3.2 Energy Balance
Without atmosphere: \[
T_{\text{eff}} = \left(\frac{(1-A)S}{4\sigma}\right)^{1/4}
\]
With greenhouse gases: \[
T_{\text{surface}} > T_{\text{eff}}
\]

text:
44.6 In Simulation
class Planet:
    def __init__(self, mass, composition):
        self.layers = differentiate(mass, composition)
        self.plates = []
        self.heat = initial_heat(mass)

    def evolve(self, dt):
        # Convection
        self.mantle_flow = convection(self.layers['mantle'])

        # Plate motion
        for plate in self.plates:
            plate.move(self.mantle_flow)

        # Volcanism
        if pressure_release(self.layers):
            create_volcano()

        # Heat loss
        self.heat -= surface_radiation(dt)

title: 46  Stellar Formation
text:
46.1 Molecular Cloud Collapse
“From nebula to star”

title: 46  Stellar Formation
text:
46.1.1 Initial Conditions
Stars form in giant molecular clouds: - Size: 10-100 parsecs - Mass: \(10^4\)-\(10^6\) \(M_\odot\) - Temperature: 10-20 K - Composition: \(\text{H}_2\), He, dust


46.1.2 Trigger Mechanisms
Something must start the collapse: - Supernova shockwave: Compression - Cloud collision: Density increase - Spiral arm compression: Density wave - Turbulence decay: Support removal


46.1.3 Jeans Criterion
Collapse occurs when gravity overcomes thermal pressure:
\[
M > M_J = \left(\frac{5k_BT}{G\mu m_H}\right)^{3/2} \left(\frac{3}{4\pi\rho}\right)^{1/2}
\]
For typical molecular cloud: \(M_J \approx 10-100 \, M_\odot\)

title: 46  Stellar Formation
text:
46.2 Fragmentation
Large clouds break into multiple protostars through hierarchical fragmentation: the initial cloud subdivides into clumps, each of which continues collapsing independently.

title: 46  Stellar Formation

46.10 Transition
Protostars become real stars when fusion ignites. Next (Chapter 47), we explore the main sequence: where stars spend most of their lives, steadily fusing hydrogen into helium for billions of years.
The journey from molecular cloud to main-sequence star takes millions of years: a geological instant on cosmic timescales, yet long enough for complex processes of fragmentation, accretion, and disk formation that determine not just stellar properties but also the planets that may form alongside.






TipRelated Topics

Stellar death: Chapter 49 explores how stars end their lives

title: 47  Main Sequence
text:
47.1 Hydrostatic Equilibrium
“Where stars spend their lives”
The balance that defines a star:
At every point in a stable star, the inward gravitational force is exactly balanced by the outward pressure from fusion reactions in the core.
\[
\frac{dP}{dr} = -\frac{Gm(r)\rho}{r^2}
\]
At every point, pressure exactly balances gravity.

title: 47  Main Sequence
text: Figure 47.1: Hydrostatic equilibrium in a star: gravity pulls inward while pressure from fusion pushes outward, creating a stable balance.

title: 47  Main Sequence
text:
47.2 Energy Generation

47.2.1 Proton-Proton Chain (M < 1.5 \(M_\odot\))
Dominant in Sun-like stars:
\[
4p \rightarrow {^4\text{He}} + 2e^+ + 2\nu_e + 26.7 \text{ MeV}
\]
Step by step:
p + p → D + e⁺ + νₑ     (slow: rate limiting)
D + p → ³He + γ
³He + ³He → ⁴He + 2p


47.2.2 CNO Cycle (M > 1.5 \(M_\odot\))
Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen catalyze fusion:
¹²C + p → ¹³N + γ
¹³N → ¹³C + e⁺ + νₑ
¹³C + p → ¹⁴N + γ
¹⁴N + p → ¹⁵O + γ     (slow: rate limiting)
¹⁵O → ¹⁵N + e⁺ + νₑ
¹⁵N + p → ¹²C + ⁴He
Net: 4p → ⁴He (carbon recycled)

title: 48  Stellar Nucleosynthesis
text:
48.2 Hydrogen Burning
Where it all starts (main sequence):
\[
4{^1\text{H}} \rightarrow {^4\text{He}} + 2e^+ + 2\nu_e + 26.7 \text{ MeV}
\]
This is the longest phase: billions of years for Sun-like stars.

title: 48  Stellar Nucleosynthesis
text:
48.3 Helium Burning

48.3.1 The Triple-Alpha Process
When hydrogen is exhausted:
\[
{^4\text{He}} + {^4\text{He}} \rightarrow {^8\text{Be}} \quad (\text{unstable, } \tau = 10^{-16} \text{ s})
\] \[
{^8\text{Be}} + {^4\text{He}} \rightarrow {^{12}\text{C}} + \gamma
\]
Requires T > 100 million K.


48.3.2 Carbon Production
The Hoyle resonance makes this possible: - \(^{12}\)C has an excited state at exactly the right energy - Without it, almost no carbon would form - Fine-tuning: Move the level by 1%, no carbon


48.3.3 Further Burning
\[
{^{12}\text{C}} + {^4\text{He}} \rightarrow {^{16}\text{O}} + \gamma
\]

48.12 Transition
Stars do not last forever. When fusion ends, stars die: sometimes quietly, sometimes explosively. Next, we explore stellar death.

title: 49  Stellar Death
text:
49.1 Low Mass Stars (< 8 \(M_\odot\))
“How stars end their lives”
The path of Sun-like stars.

title: 49  Stellar Death
text:
49.1.1 Red Giant Phase
When core hydrogen exhausted: 1. Core contracts, heats 2. Shell burning begins 3. Envelope expands 4. Surface cools → red 5. Star swells to ~100× original size


49.1.2 Helium Flash
In stars < 2 \(M_\odot\): - Degenerate core ignites helium - Runaway fusion (seconds) - Core expands, stabilizes


49.1.3 Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB)
After helium exhausted: - Double shell burning (H and He) - Thermal pulses - Strong mass loss - Planetary nebula forms


49.1.4 Planetary Nebula
The expelled envelope forms a planetary nebula: an expanding shell of gas illuminated by ultraviolet radiation from the hot central star. These beautiful objects persist for tens of thousands of years before dispersing into the interstellar medium.


49.1.5 White Dwarf
What remains: - Carbon-oxygen core - ~0.6 \(M_\odot\) typically - Earth-sized - Electron degeneracy pressure - Slowly cools forever

title: 49  Stellar Death
text:
49.2 High Mass Stars (> 8 \(M_\odot\))
The path to supernova.

49.2.1 Pre-Supernova
Multiple burning stages create onion structure: - Each stage shorter than the last - Iron core grows - Silicon burning lasts only days


49.2.2 Core Collapse
When iron core exceeds Chandrasekhar mass (~1.4 \(M_\odot\)): 1. Electron degeneracy fails 2. Core collapses in milliseconds 3. Neutronization: p + e\(^-\) \(\to\) n + \(\nu_e\) 4. Core bounces at nuclear density 5. Shock wave launches


49.2.3 The Explosion
Energy release: approximately \(10^{46}\) J, with 99% carried away by neutrinos. The remaining 1% drives the explosion, launching the stellar envelope outward at speeds up to 10,000 km/s.






Figure 49.1: The pathways of stellar death: low-mass stars become white dwarfs via red giant and planetary nebula phases, while massive stars explode as supernovae leaving neutron stars or black holes.

49.3.1 Mechanism
White dwarf in binary system: 1. Accretes matter from companion 2. Approaches 1.4 \(M_\odot\) 3. Carbon ignites throughout 4. Entire star explodes


49.3.2 Standard Candles
All Type Ia have similar peak luminosity: - Used to measure cosmic distances - Led to discovery of dark energy

title: 50  Compact Objects

50.1 White Dwarfs
“The endpoints of stellar evolution”
The end state of Sun-like stars.

50.1.1 Properties

50.1.2 Electron Degeneracy
Pauli exclusion: no two electrons in same state - Electrons fill up to Fermi energy - Pressure from exclusion principle - Independent of temperature


50.1.3 Chandrasekhar Limit
\[
M_{\text{Ch}} = 1.44 \, M_\odot
\]
Above this mass, electron degeneracy fails.


50.1.4 Cooling
White dwarfs are born hot and cool over billions of years: - No energy generation - Radiate stored thermal energy - Eventually become black dwarfs (not yet: universe too young)

title: 50  Compact Objects
text:
50.2 Neutron Stars
When electron degeneracy fails.

50.2.1 Formation
In core collapse: \[
p + e^- \rightarrow n + \nu_e
\]
Protons and electrons combine into neutrons.


50.2.2 Properties

50.2.3 Structure






Figure 50.1: The internal structure of compact objects: white dwarfs supported by electron degeneracy, neutron stars with their exotic layered interiors, and black holes defined by their event horizons.



A neutron star has distinct layers: an outer crust of iron lattice and electrons, an inner crust of neutron-rich nuclei with free neutrons dripping out, an outer core of superfluid neutrons and superconducting protons, and a mysterious inner core that may contain exotic quark matter.


50.2.4 Pulsars
Rotating neutron stars with beamed radiation emit like cosmic lighthouses. Their magnetic axes are typically misaligned with their rotation axes, causing the beams to sweep across space. When Earth lies in the beam’s path, we detect regular pulses.

Periods: milliseconds to seconds
Extremely regular (some rival atomic clocks)
Slow down gradually as rotational energy is radiated away



50.2.5 Magnetars
Neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields: - B ~ \(10^{14}\)-\(10^{15}\) G - Occasional giant flares - Most magnetized objects known

title: 50  Compact Objects
text:
50.3 Black Holes
When nothing can resist gravity.

50.3.1 Formation
From core collapse of very massive stars (>25 \(M_\odot\)).


50.3.2 Event Horizon
Schwarzschild radius: \[
r_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2} \approx 3 \text{ km} \times \frac{M}{M_\odot}
\]
Nothing, not even light, escapes from within.

50.3.4 Properties (Kerr Black Hole)
Rotating black holes have: - Event horizon (smaller than non-rotating) - Ergosphere (region where space is dragged) - Ring singularity (not a point)


50.3.5 Information Paradox
Quantum mechanics says information cannot be destroyed. Black holes seem to destroy information. Resolution: Hawking radiation? Holography?

title: 50  Compact Objects
text:
50.4 Hawking Radiation
Black holes emit thermal radiation:
\[
T_H = \frac{\hbar c^3}{8\pi G M k_B} \approx 6 \times 10^{-8} \text{ K} \times \frac{M_\odot}{M}
\]

Virtual pairs at horizon: one escapes, one falls in
Black holes slowly evaporate
For stellar mass: timescale >> age of universe

title: 51  Galaxy Formation

51.2 The Role of Dark Matter
Dark matter dominates structure formation: - Does not interact with light (no pressure) - Collapses first - Creates gravitational wells - Baryons fall in later

51.2.1 The Cosmic Web
Dark matter forms a web-like structure: dense nodes (galaxy clusters) connected by filaments, with vast voids in between. Galaxies form at the intersection points where dark matter halos concentrate.






Figure 51.1: The cosmic web structure: dark matter halos at nodes and along filaments, with galaxies forming in the densest regions.

title: 51  Galaxy Formation
text:
51.3 Formation Pathways

51.3.1 Hierarchical Merging (Modern View)






Figure 51.2: Galaxy formation pathways: from small dark matter halos in the early universe through hierarchical merging to present-day galaxies.



In this bottom-up process, small halos form first and progressively merge into larger structures over cosmic time.


51.3.2 Bottom-Up Process

Dark matter halos form (z ~ 20-30)
Gas falls in (cools, condenses)
First stars form (z ~ 20)
Small galaxies merge (z ~ 10-2)
Continued growth (ongoing)

title: 51  Galaxy Formation
text:
51.4 Gas Cooling and Star Formation

51.4.1 Cooling Time
Gas must cool to collapse: \[
t_{\text{cool}} = \frac{3k_BT n}{2 \Lambda(T) n^2}
\]
Where Λ(T) is the cooling function.
If \(t_{\text{cool}} < t_{\text{Hubble}}\): gas can cool, collapse, form stars.


51.4.2 The Cooling Curve
Gas cools most efficiently at temperatures between \(10^4\) and \(10^6\) K, where atomic line cooling dominates. Above this range, bremsstrahlung (free-free emission) takes over but is less efficient. Below it, the gas becomes neutral and cooling rates drop sharply.

title: 51  Galaxy Formation
text:
51.5 Angular Momentum
Galaxies spin because: - Tidal torques from neighbors - Random motions during collapse - Conservation of angular momentum

51.5.1 Disk Formation
Gas with angular momentum settles into disk: - Falls to center - Spins up (conservation) - Flattens perpendicular to rotation axis

title: 51  Galaxy Formation
text:

51.6.1 Stellar Feedback

Supernovae heat and expel gas
Stellar winds inject energy
UV radiation ionizes gas



51.6.2 AGN Feedback

Central black hole accretes
Jets and outflows
Can quench star formation

        # Gas cools
        if cooling_time(gas) < hubble_time():
            gas.cool()
            gas.condense()

        # Stars form from dense gas

        feedback(central_black_hole, gas)

Binary hardens (ejects stars)

Eventually merge → gravitational waves

54.6.1 Ram Pressure Stripping
In galaxy clusters, galaxies moving through the hot intracluster medium experience ram pressure that strips gas from their disks, like wind blowing through a dandelion. This can completely remove a galaxy’s gas reservoir, quenching star formation.






Figure 54.1: Galaxy merger sequence: from initial approach through tidal distortion, starburst, and final coalescence into an elliptical remnant.





54.6.2 Harassment
Repeated high-speed encounters in clusters: - Heats disk stars - Thickens disk - Eventually transforms spiral → S0


54.6.3 Strangulation
Cut off from fresh gas supply: - Existing gas consumed - No new star formation - Slow fading to red

56.1 Evidence for Dark Matter

title: 56  Dark Matter
text:
56.1.1 Galaxy Rotation Curves
Expected (Keplerian): \[
v(r) \propto r^{-1/2}
\]
Observed: \[
v(r) \approx \text{constant at large } r
\]






Figure 56.1: Evidence for dark matter: rotation curves show flat velocities at large radii instead of the expected Keplerian decline.



This discrepancy between expected and observed rotation curves requires additional unseen mass.


56.1.2 Galaxy Cluster Masses
Multiple methods give consistent results: - Virial theorem: \(M = \frac{3\sigma^2 R}{G}\) - X-ray gas: Hydrostatic equilibrium - Gravitational lensing: Light bending
All give: \(M_{\text{total}} >> M_{\text{visible}}\)


56.1.3 Gravitational Lensing
Mass bends light: - Strong lensing: Multiple images, arcs - Weak lensing: Statistical distortions - Maps invisible mass directly


56.1.4 The Bullet Cluster
Two clusters collided, providing smoking-gun evidence for dark matter. The galaxies passed through each other largely unaffected. The hot gas collided and was left behind at the collision point. But gravitational lensing reveals that most of the mass (dark matter) passed through like the galaxies, now separated from the gas. This proves dark matter is a distinct component from ordinary matter.


56.1.5 CMB Anisotropies
Pattern of fluctuations requires dark matter: - Baryons alone do not match - Need ~5× more non-baryonic matter - Confirmed by Planck satellite
